entities.name: Establish personal dominance and power
entities.evidence_basis: At nine years old, he already understood power as something to be seized, not requested. Learned that affection must be earned through competence and dominance, not expected through sentiment.

entities.name: Liberate Corsica from French occupation
entities.evidence_basis: He revered Paoli, the Corsican patriot his father had abandoned, and fantasised about liberating Corsica himself.

entities.name: Build strength and competence as path to affection
entities.evidence_basis: The lesson Napoleon absorbed was specific: affection must be earned through competence and dominance, not expected through sentiment. Love was not unconditional — it was the reward for strength, not a right conferred by birth.

entities.name: Obtain French military education and credentials
entities.evidence_basis: Carlo secured scholarships for his sons at French military academies.

entities.name: Internalize maternal discipline as character foundation
entities.evidence_basis: My mother's firmness prevented my ruin. She expected obedience and administered punishment with an impartiality that bordered on coldness. Napoleon would later describe this as the foundation of his character.

entities.name: Maintain emotional distance and self-reliance

entities.name: Convert shame and rejection into contempt and determination
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon responded not with tears but with a cold, watchful fury. He converted his isolation into a fortress of contempt.

entities.name: Achieve greatness and historical significance

entities.name: Rise through merit rather than aristocratic birth

entities.name: Achieve rapid military advancement and recognition

entities.name: Secure romantic devotion and emotional validation from Joséphine
entities.evidence_basis: He wrote daily letters with intense passion during the Italian campaign: 'I awake filled with you.' He was 'abject, desperate, jealous — a man who commanded armies reduced to begging a woman for a letter.' The asymmetry between his frequent writing and her infrequent, indifferent replies 'tormented him.'

entities.name: Obtain approval and admiration from Joséphine as validation of personal importance
entities.evidence_basis: He 'wanted Joséphine not as a partner but as an audience for his greatness, a mirror that would reflect back his importance.' His need for her approval 'directly contradicted everything he believed about self-sufficiency,' suggesting an unconscious dependency masked by ideals of independence.

entities.name: Maintain control and possession of Joséphine as an extension of self
entities.evidence_basis: His love was 'possessive and controlling' — he wanted her as 'an audience for his greatness' rather than a partner. When she failed to comply (taking lovers, spending money), 'his pain was genuine but his response was rage, not reflection.' He 'could not understand why someone would not want to be consumed by him.'

entities.name: Achieve military dominance and political power
entities.evidence_basis: By age twenty-six, Napoleon had suppressed the royalist uprising and 'was rewarded with command of the Army of the Interior,' becoming 'suddenly powerful, suddenly visible.' He then left to command the Italian campaign, demonstrating sustained pursuit of military expansion and authority.

entities.name: Create permanent institutional bond with Joséphine through marriage
entities.evidence_basis: They married on 9 March 1796, two days before Napoleon left for Italy. The marriage certificate falsified both their ages 'as though the relationship could only exist in a shared fiction,' suggesting the marriage was formalized to bind her to him despite emotional distance.

entities.name: Military dominance and battlefield superiority
entities.evidence_basis: He was 'happy in a way that only victory made possible.' Each battle confirmed his superiority and validated his self-estimation. The passage emphasizes his tactical brilliance and his personal charge at Lodi, suggesting victory is his primary source of satisfaction.

entities.name: Recognition and vindication of personal superiority
entities.evidence_basis: The passage notes: 'Each defeated general was evidence that the world's estimation of talent was finally, belatedly, aligning with his own.' This reveals a deep need to prove that his self-assessment was correct all along, despite initial officer contempt for his age, stature, and Corsican origin.

entities.name: Achieve and consolidate personal power independent of authority
entities.evidence_basis: He 'ignored' Directory orders, 'marginalised' commissioners, negotiated treaties without authorization, reorganized Italian states without permission. The passage states: 'the men in Paris who had given him this army as a consolation prize now depended on him for their survival. The reversal gave him a pleasure that was almost physical.'

entities.name: Transform demoralized army into an effective fighting force
entities.evidence_basis: Upon arrival, the army was 'starving, unpaid, and demoralised.' Within weeks, 'he had transformed them' through 'tactical brilliance, relentless energy, and a gift for inspirational rhetoric.' The soldiers began calling him 'le petit caporal' with 'affection and awe.'

entities.name: Acquire territorial and material wealth through military conquest
entities.evidence_basis: His recruitment pitch to soldiers promised: 'I will lead you into the most fertile plains in the world. Rich provinces, great cities will be in your power.' The passage notes this was 'a promise of loot dressed as liberation.' He sent back 'looted art as fait accompli' without authorization.

entities.name: Suppress potential rival commanders and eliminate threats to supremacy
entities.evidence_basis: When Bernadotte displayed 'independent ambition,' Napoleon 'froze him out.' When Bernadotte won without orders, Napoleon did not congratulate him but 'reassigned him.' The passage generalizes: 'subordinates who succeeded too visibly were threats, not allies' and 'confronted with a rival's actual success, his instinct was suppression, not celebration.'

entities.name: Win decisive military victories in rapid succession
entities.evidence_basis: He 'destroyed the Austrians and Sardinians in a series of battles — Montenotte, Lodi, Arcole, Rivoli — that became legendary for their speed and audacity.' He personally led the charge at Lodi under fire.

entities.name: Follow in Alexander the Great's footsteps
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon wanted to follow in Alexander's footsteps. He wanted to add 'conqueror of the East' to his identity.

entities.name: Conquer and possess the East intellectually and militarily
entities.evidence_basis: He intended not merely to conquer but to understand, to catalogue, to possess intellectually as well as militarily.

entities.name: Threaten British India and establish French influence in eastern Mediterranean
entities.evidence_basis: The expedition was ostensibly strategic — to threaten British India and establish French influence in the eastern Mediterranean

entities.name: Understand Egypt through scholarly and scientific study
entities.evidence_basis: He took a library of books on Egypt, Islam, and ancient history. He intended not merely to conquer but to understand, to catalogue, to possess intellectually as well as militarily. The scientific expedition, the Description de l'Égypte, the founding of the Institut d'Égypte — all were real achievements.

entities.name: Establish and maintain personal dominance in intimate relationships
entities.evidence_basis: His response was not introspection but retaliation: he took a mistress, Pauline Fourès, the wife of a junior officer, with a brazenness that humiliated the husband and established a principle Napoleon would maintain for life — that fidelity was a obligation he imposed on others, not one he accepted for himself.

entities.name: Protect emotional vulnerability through emotional distance
entities.evidence_basis: The hurt was real, but what he learned from it was not empathy but armour. His response was not introspection but retaliation.

entities.name: Manage military and personal setbacks through propaganda and narrative control
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon managed these setbacks with a combination of genuine tactical adaptation and shameless propaganda: the scientific expedition, the Description de l'Égypte, the founding of the Institut d'Égypte — all were real achievements designed to conceal a military stalemate.

entities.name: Secure power in France
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon abandoned Egypt claiming 'France needed him more than Egypt did.' He believed he 'could do better' than the weak Directory and was 'certain that if he waited, someone else would seize the opportunity.' Successfully executed the coup of 18 Brumaire to become First Consul.

entities.name: Prevent rival seizure of opportunity
entities.evidence_basis: He was 'certain that if he waited, someone else would seize the opportunity,' motivating his urgent departure from Egypt and execution of the coup in November 1799.

entities.name: Maintain a commanding self-image
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'hated the memory of his own incompetence' at the coup and systematically replaced the true account with a version 'that matched his self-image.' He possessed a 'capacity for self-mythologising — for believing his own propaganda' that operated as 'a mind that genuinely could not tolerate its own failure.'

entities.name: Suppress acknowledgment of dependency and failure
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'never acknowledged that Lucien had saved the coup' despite his brother rallying grenadiers and engineering the constitutional changes. Instead, he retold events 'often' with himself as 'calm, commanding, decisive,' demonstrating consistent psychological replacement of uncomfortable truths.

entities.name: Establish France's military and political superiority
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon justified abandoning Egypt by stating 'France needed him more,' implying a goal to restore French strength. The Directory was 'weak, corrupt, and militarily failing,' and he was 'certain he could do better,' indicating intent to reform France's condition.

entities.name: Establish lasting legal legacy
entities.evidence_basis: "My true glory is not in having won forty battles. Waterloo will wipe out the memory of those victories. What nothing can destroy, what will live forever, is my Civil Code."

entities.name: Transform French governance through rational systematization
entities.evidence_basis: Reorganised tax system, established Bank of France, built roads and canals, created lycée system, codified French law; worked eighteen-hour days with revolutionary energy

entities.name: Embed rationality, order, and clarity into French institutions
entities.evidence_basis: The Code was an expression of his deepest values: rationality, order, clarity, meritocracy

entities.name: Establish patriarchal social order with male authority
entities.evidence_basis: The Code stripped women of legal autonomy, subordinated wives to husbands, made divorce difficult for women and easy for men. Women belonged in domestic sphere; men in public one.

entities.name: Secure social stability through religious legitimacy
entities.evidence_basis: Reconciled with Catholic Church through Concordat of 1801, not from religious belief but because he understood social control required spiritual legitimacy: "Society cannot exist without inequality of fortunes, and inequality of fortunes cannot exist without religion."

entities.name: Alleviate poverty and suffering through centralized personal authority
entities.evidence_basis: He was genuinely moved by the suffering he saw in the provinces; believed his empathy combined with power made him uniquely capable of fixing it

entities.name: Exercise supreme personal authority over French state
entities.evidence_basis: His empathy was always channelled through conviction that he, and only he, knew how to fix society's problems; believed power without sympathy was tyranny and only he had both

entities.name: Control and manage women through legal and personal authority
entities.evidence_basis: His own experience with Joséphine's infidelity and Letizia's iron discipline taught him women were either to be controlled or to be feared; Code reflected both lessons

entities.name: Achieve international legal influence through Code adoption
entities.evidence_basis: Civil Code would eventually be adopted or adapted by dozens of nations

entities.name: Establish absolute personal sovereignty
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon deliberately took the crown from the altar and placed it on his own head at coronation; the gesture explicitly communicated 'he owed his throne to no one, not even God'—demonstrating a core aspiration to absolute self-determined authority independent of institutional or divine validation.

entities.name: Achieve supreme military dominance through tactical brilliance
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon deliberately engineered the Battle of Austerlitz through deception (weakening right flank as bait), perfect timing, and strategic strike at centre. His characterization of it as 'the finest of all I have fought' and explicit comparison to prior battles reveals sustained pursuit of tactical perfection.

entities.name: Validate self-conception through external proof of superiority
entities.evidence_basis: After Austerlitz, Napoleon experienced 'deep, settled satisfaction that came from the confirmation of everything he believed about himself.' The passage states: 'Austerlitz was not just a victory. It was proof.' This reveals an underlying need to convert internal belief into external validation.

entities.name: Maintain intimate emotional connection with Joséphine despite instrumental considerations
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'relented at the last moment' from divorcing Joséphine despite the political pressure (she had not given him an heir). At coronation, he displayed 'genuine tenderness' and 'gentleness,' which observers noted contrasted with his private humiliation of her, suggesting he actively preserved the relationship despite competing dynastic needs.

entities.name: Secure dynastic legitimacy through heir production
entities.evidence_basis: The passage notes Napoleon 'had almost divorced her the year before — she had not given him an heir,' indicating pressure to produce succession. His eventual decision to retain Joséphine despite this impediment suggests the goal remains active but is now subordinated to intimacy goals.

entities.name: Exercise benevolent ownership and control over subordinates
entities.evidence_basis: After Austerlitz, viewing the battlefield dead and wounded, Napoleon remarked: 'These are my children.' The passage notes 'there was compassion in the remark — and also ownership. He was sorry for their suffering, but their suffering was evidence of his achievement.' This reveals a goal to maintain paternalistic authority coupled with emotional investment.

entities.name: Establish Continental dominance and control
entities.evidence_basis: Austerlitz made Napoleon master of Europe; he redrew the map with casual authority, abolished the Holy Roman Empire, created the Confederation of the Rhine, and installed brothers on thrones across the continent.

entities.name: Enforce the Continental System to isolate Britain economically
entities.evidence_basis: He imposed the Continental System — a trade blockade against Britain that required every European nation to close its ports to British goods. The policy required military enforcement that stretched French resources and rested on the assumption that Napoleon could control the entire European coastline.

entities.name: Ensure absolute loyalty and obedience from family members
entities.evidence_basis: When his brothers proved incompetent or disloyal, he berated them with fury. He wrote to Louis: 'You are a king, and you forget that you are a French prince.' To Jérôme: 'You give up the substance for the shadow. Your conduct disgusts me.' This revealed his inability to accept that other Bonapartes were not replicas of himself.

entities.name: Maintain infallibility and suppress contradictory information
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon could not distinguish between what he wanted to be true and what was true. He dismissed bad news, punished advisers who delivered it, and surrounded himself with men who told him what he wanted to hear. He humiliated Talleyrand publicly, calling him 'a silk stocking full of excrement' for warning that the Continental System was unsustainable.

entities.name: Exercise will-power as ultimate problem-solving mechanism
entities.evidence_basis: He believed there was no problem his will could not solve. This belief underlay his redrawing of Europe, the Continental System, and his dismissal of evidence that Spain was unconquerable, Russia was ignoring the blockade, and Austria was rearming.

entities.evidence_basis: He predicted a quick campaign: one or two decisive battles, a humbled Tsar, a return to Paris before winter.

entities.name: Achieve decisive military victory through battle
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon advanced, waiting for the decisive battle that never came. Borodino was a pyrrhic victory... but the Russian army was not destroyed.

entities.name: Compel Russian surrender through presence in Moscow
entities.evidence_basis: He could not accept that his presence in Moscow was not, by itself, sufficient to compel surrender.

entities.name: Return to Paris before winter
entities.evidence_basis: a humbled Tsar, a return to Paris before winter

lifecycle.context: Temperatures drop to minus thirty degrees during retreat; soldiers freeze to death

entities.name: Maintain military cohesion during catastrophic retreat
entities.evidence_basis: He organised the rearguard with genuine tactical skill, maintaining enough cohesion to prevent total disintegration.

entities.name: Save soldiers' lives during river crossings and retreat
entities.evidence_basis: He walked among the soldiers, shared their cold, and made decisions that saved thousands who would otherwise have died at the river crossings.

entities.name: Secure France's future through personal return to Paris
entities.evidence_basis: France needed him more than the army did. When he finally abandoned the army in December — riding ahead to Paris in a sleigh — he justified it the same way.

entities.name: Rapidly rebuild military force to counter coalition powers
entities.evidence_basis: he needed to raise a new army before the coalition powers exploited his weakness.

entities.name: Control narrative and minimize perceived responsibility for disaster
entities.evidence_basis: He dictated bulletins to Paris that minimised the disaster, blamed the weather, blamed the Russians, blamed everything except his own decision to invade.

entities.name: Achieve redemption or moral reconciliation through retrospective empathy
entities.evidence_basis: At St Helena, he would weep when he spoke of the retreat. 'Those poor fellows. They suffered so much.' He was sorry for them — retrospectively, safely, from the distance of exile.

entities.name: Preserve and expand imperial dominion
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon refused to accept loss of conquered territories and rejected generous peace terms that would preserve France's natural borders and his throne, stating 'I cannot. I was not raised to such a throne to accept limitations.'

entities.name: Maintain personal invincibility and supremacy
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'genuinely could not see that a smaller empire voluntarily accepted was preferable to a larger empire violently lost' and believed acceptance meant 'admitting he was not the man he believed himself to be.'

entities.name: Reject negotiated peace and continue military struggle
entities.evidence_basis: Despite advisers urging peace and allies offering generous terms at Prague in summer 1813 (allowing France to keep Belgium, Rhineland, and northern Italy), 'Napoleon refused' and 'could not accept it because acceptance meant acknowledging limits.'

entities.name: Reorganize forces and mount counterattacks
entities.evidence_basis: After Leipzig defeat, 'He planned counterattacks, dictated orders, reorganised what remained of his forces' despite tactical impossibility.

entities.name: Shape and control fate through will and action
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'had spent his entire career believing he could shape fate' but for the first time recognized 'that fate might shape him.' This lifelong conviction about controlling destiny is central to his resistance to compromise.

entities.name: Avoid acknowledgement of human limitation and fallibility
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon refuses peace because 'acceptance meant acknowledging limits, and acknowledging limits meant admitting he was not the man he believed himself to be.' His psychological architecture rejects recognition of constraint.

entities.name: Maintain emotional connection with loyal followers
entities.evidence_basis: At Fontainebleau, Napoleon addressed his Old Guard in a farewell ceremony and embraced Marshal Petit, gestures that reduced hardened soldiers to tears. He prioritized personal connection with his loyal troops at the moment of abdication.

entities.name: Escape the annihilation of lost power and identity
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon's suicide attempt revealed that 'his sense of self was entirely dependent on his power. Without the empire, he was not diminished — he was annihilated. He could not imagine a life in which he was merely a man.' This demonstrates his core existential goal to avoid the dissolution of his identity.

entities.name: Restore lost imperial power and dominion
entities.evidence_basis: After his recovery on Elba, 'Within months, he was planning his return.' This indicates a sustained directional goal to reclaim his empire, driven by his inability to accept diminished status.

entities.name: Remain productively engaged and mentally active
entities.evidence_basis: On Elba, 'He recovered with characteristic speed. He reorganised the island's finances, built roads, improved the iron mines, and drilled his small garrison. He was a man who could not be idle.' This demonstrates a core need for purposeful activity and competent action.

entities.name: Improve governance of territory under his control
entities.evidence_basis: On Elba, Napoleon 'reorganised the island's finances, built roads, improved the iron mines, and drilled his small garrison,' demonstrating concrete administrative objectives despite his constrained situation.

entities.name: Survive existential despair and find meaning to continue living
entities.evidence_basis: After his failed suicide attempt, Napoleon told his valet: 'God has decided I must continue to suffer.' This reflects acceptance of a goal to endure and survive despite the annihilation of his former identity.

entities.name: Return to power and reclaim the throne
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon landed with 1,000 men, marched north toward Paris, and entered the Tuileries on 20 March. The passage states 'He was back. He was Emperor.'

entities.name: Secure loyalty and support through narrative and spectacle
entities.evidence_basis: At Laffrey, Napoleon 'opened his coat to their muskets' and declared himself, understanding 'that men will follow a story they believe in, even against their orders.' The regiment defected to him, shouting 'Vive l'Empereur!'

entities.name: Govern as a constitutional monarch with liberal reforms
entities.evidence_basis: Upon entering the Tuileries, 'He promised liberal reforms, a new constitution, peace with Europe.' The passage notes 'He genuinely wanted to govern as a constitutional monarch' but this was 'not credible' and the goal ultimately failed.

entities.name: Achieve international acceptance and peace with European powers
entities.evidence_basis: He 'promised...peace with Europe' and 'genuinely believed the allies would accept his return.' However, he 'was wrong' because 'the Europe of 1815 would not tolerate him regardless of what he promised.'

entities.name: Experience the drama and risk of historic adventure
entities.evidence_basis: The passage describes how 'The adventure itself was the drug — the risk, the drama, the confirmation that he was the protagonist of history.' His happiness during the Hundred Days derived from this experiential goal.

entities.name: Confirm himself as the protagonist and central agent of history
entities.evidence_basis: The passage explicitly states the Hundred Days provided 'confirmation that he was the protagonist of history.' This recurring need for validation frames his entire campaign.

entities.name: Defeat Wellington and the Anglo-allied army
entities.evidence_basis: His plan was sound: fix Wellington in place, then crush him with the Imperial Guard before Blücher's Prussians could arrive.

entities.name: Prevent Prussian reinforcements from arriving at Waterloo
entities.evidence_basis: crush him with the Imperial Guard before Blücher's Prussians could arrive; Marshal Grouchy failed to prevent Blücher's approach.

entities.name: Preserve personal control and authority through blame-shifting
entities.evidence_basis: He raged at Ney. He cursed Grouchy. He blamed everyone except himself for the deteriorating situation.

entities.name: Maintain belief in personal superiority and centrality
entities.evidence_basis: He still believed he was the most important person in any room, any country, any century.

entities.name: Secure asylum and favorable historical narrative after defeat
entities.evidence_basis: He fled to Paris, abdicated for the second time on 22 June, and surrendered to the British on 15 July, boarding HMS Bellerophon with a letter to the Prince Regent in which he compared himself to Themistocles.

entities.name: Justify surrender through historical analogy and self-comparison
entities.evidence_basis: boarding HMS Bellerophon with a letter to the Prince Regent in which he compared himself to Themistocles — the Athenian general who had sought asylum from his former enemy. The comparison was grandiose, self-serving, and — in its way — not entirely wrong.

entities.name: Maintain sense of self amid imprisonment and defeat
entities.evidence_basis: The passage describes Napoleon's construction of alternative narratives as 'the construction of a narrative that allowed him to maintain his sense of self in conditions that should have destroyed it.'

entities.name: Construct a historical legacy that preserves personal honor
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'dictated his memoirs...and in doing so, he constructed the myth that would outlive the man. He rewrote his defeats as misfortunes, his mistakes as betrayals, his ambition as patriotism.'

entities.name: Rewrite military defeats as external misfortunes rather than personal errors
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'rewrote his defeats as misfortunes, his mistakes as betrayals' and blamed Waterloo 'because of Grouchy, or Ney, or the rain, or fate — never because Napoleon had miscalculated.'

entities.name: Assert authority and dignity through resistance to Lowe's administration
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'fought over everything — the size of the garden, the quality of the wine, the number of guards, whether Napoleon should be addressed as "Emperor" or "General Bonaparte." Napoleon was fighting the only battles still available to him.'

entities.name: Escape psychological destruction through belief in alternative reality
entities.evidence_basis: The passage describes how 'If Napoleon admitted that Russia was a mistake...The weight of that admission would have been unbearable. So he built an alternative history...and believed it with the same intensity he had believed in his military plans.'

entities.name: Reframe imperial campaigns as righteous missions rather than acts of aggression
entities.evidence_basis: Napoleon 'rewrote his defeats as misfortunes...The Egyptian campaign became a civilising mission. The Spanish war became a defensive necessity.'

entities.name: Reconnect with and raise his son
entities.evidence_basis: He spoke often of his son, whom he had not seen since 1814. Napoleon's grief over this separation was the most unguarded emotion of his exile. 'I would have loved him,' he said. 'I would have made him a man.' The conditional tense was the saddest thing about it: he was mourning not what he had lost but what he had never had.

entities.name: Establish and preserve order over chaos
entities.evidence_basis: He reflected on what he had built and what it had cost. 'I closed the gulf of anarchy and brought order out of chaos,' he said. 'I am the French Revolution.' He had preserved the Revolution's legal and administrative achievements while extinguishing its democratic aspirations. Whether this was a rescue or a betrayal depended on whether you valued order or liberty — and Napoleon, to the end, valued order.

entities.name: Control his historical narrative and legacy
entities.evidence_basis: He had spent his last years making sure that the story of that trajectory would be told on his terms. He succeeded. The myth he built at St Helena — of the martyred Emperor, the champion of the people, the man betrayed by lesser men — proved more durable than any of his military victories.

entities.name: Achieve spiritual reconciliation before death
entities.evidence_basis: He reconciled with the Church, receiving last rites from a priest.

entities.name: Find peace and acceptance in exile through simple pleasures
entities.evidence_basis: He spent hours in the garden, tending plants. He read novels. He played cards. The restless energy that had defined him was gone.

memories.text: Napoleon was born in Ajaccio, Corsica on 15 August 1769, one year after the island's cession from Genoa to France. His father Carlo Buonaparte had fought for Corsican independence under Pasquale Paoli before pragmatically switching allegiance to the French Crown.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is slightly negative due to the ambivalent context of colonial displacement and paternal compromise—a foundational tension rather than joyful origin. Arousal is low (0.2) because this is a biographical fact being recounted, not an immediate experience, though the political backdrop adds subtle tension. Dominance is negative (-0.4) because the newborn has no agency and is born into a colonized territory whose political fate was decided by others.

cognitive.occ_emotions_justification: Interest (0.6) is attributed to the infant's later curiosity about power and identity, foreshadowed by the politically charged circumstances. Resentment (0.5) is attributed retrospectively—the passage suggests Napoleon later resented his father's pragmatic accommodation, and this memory encodes that foundational contradiction.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance (0.95) is extremely high—birth defines all subsequent identity and trajectory. Novelty (0.7) is moderately high because the timing (post-cession) is historically contingent, not inevitable. Urgency (0.4) is moderate; while birth is foundational, the narrative urgency lies in the political backdrop, not the biological event itself. Conduciveness (0.1) is slightly positive because the French cession paradoxically enabled Carlo's social climbing and access to French military schools, despite its political cost. Controllability and adjustability (0.0) are absent—birth circumstances are fully determined by prior events. Internal standards (0.3) reflect the later Napoleonic value of strength and earned dominance, which this memory subtly introduces as a theme. External standards (0.85) are high because the narrative is heavily weighted toward objective historical facts (dates, names, political allegiances) and Corsican/French cultural norms of pragmatism.

action_tendencies.action_tendencies_justification: Dominant tendency is attendance (0.65)—the memory establishes a biographical fact requiring acknowledgment and integration into identity. Secondary approach (0.4) reflects the later drive to leverage or exploit the circumstances (French education, French power structures), foreshadowed in Carlo's opportunism.

sub_thoughts.text: Born into political displacement and parental contradiction—a founding ambivalence
Corsica's cession to France created the condition for Carlo's pragmatic shift, enabling access to French institutions
Carlo's accommodation is simultaneously pragmatic (securing advancement) and morally compromised (abandoning patriotic ideals)
Napoleon will later channel the contradiction into a drive for absolute power—to resolve what his father could not
I am born of compromise, but I need not be bound by it; I can seize power rather than negotiate for it
Birth timing links to Pasquale Paoli (the patriot father rejected) and to later fantasy of Corsican liberation
What does it mean that I owe my opportunity to the very system my family resists?

cognitive.cognitive_distortions_justification: Mind-reading (0.55) appears in the retrospective attribution of Napoleon's later resentment onto the infant memory—we assume he 'understood' or 'despised' at birth what he only understood later. The passage conflates infant experience with adult interpretation.

drive_impact.drive_justification: Curiosity (+0.5) is seeded by the politically charged, ambiguous context. Competence (+0.6) is primed by Carlo's social climbing and the narrative of earned advantage through education. Affiliation (-0.3) is slightly suppressed because love is presented as conditional, not given. Autonomy (-0.7) is strongly suppressed—birth is the ultimate non-choice, born into colonization, dependent on parental decisions, denied control over circumstances.

confidence.confidence_justification: Confidence is very high (0.95) because the core facts are historically documented: birth date, location, parents' names, and Carlo's political trajectory are all verifiable. The interpretation of Napoleon's later emotional state ('despised', 'revered') is less certain but is explicitly attributed in the source text.

habituation.echoes: Being born into political ambivalence and parental contradiction is highly novel; it will echo throughout Napoleon's adult need to resolve the tension between exploitation and liberation, pragmatism and idealism.

cognitive.caps_inputs_justification: Relationship_loss (0.4): implicit loss of Pasquale Paoli's patriotic cause. Social_threat (0.5): born into a recently conquered territory. Autonomy_choice_restricted (0.8): no agency in birth circumstances. Autonomy_routine_established (0.3): the household structure and French education path are being set. Social_group_exclusion (0.4): Corsican identity is being subsumed into French identity.

goal_impacts.goal: Prove strength and dominance beyond parental pragmatism
Resolve the contradiction between exploitation and idealism

cognitive.relationship_justification: The relationship begins with pragmatic benefit (education, advancement) but is shadowed by later resentment of Carlo's accommodation with French occupiers. Trust trajectory is decreasing because the narrative frames Carlo's pragmatism as morally compromised, creating dissonance that Napoleon will not resolve in his father's lifetime.

gut_feeling.resonance: Born into compromise, raised by emotional severity—safety is conditional, not assured.

memories.text: Napoleon developed a relationship with his father Carlo Buonaparte characterized by pragmatic benefit but moral contradiction: he despised Carlo's accommodation with French occupation while accepting the French military education and noble credentials Carlo had secured for him.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is high: family identity and moral positioning are core to self-concept. Controllability is low because Napoleon cannot undo Carlo's collaboration or reject the education without social cost. Internal standards are violated (moral contradiction), while external standards reward pragmatism and noble status.

Accept the material advantages while maintaining psychological distance; differentiate self from father's moral compromises through superior ideological positioning
Napoleon is complicit in the same pragmatism he despises in Carlo—he benefits from collaboration he publicly opposes, raising questions about his own integrity
This contradiction echoes broader tensions between nationalist ideology and French institutional power; between personal ambition and moral principle

memories.text: Napoleon was sent to Collège d'Autun in January 1779 speaking only Corsican Italian, where French boys mocked his accent, small stature, poverty, and foreignness. While his brother Joseph adapted, Napoleon refused to assimilate and converted his isolation into contempt for his peers.

memories.situation_types: rejection, social_threat, social_exclusion, criticism_received, novelty_encountered, choice_available

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is negative due to mocking and rejection; arousal is elevated (0.75) because social exclusion and mockery generate acute emotional activation, not mere routine distress; dominance is negative because Napoleon lacks social power in this context, though he attempts to reclaim it through contempt.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is extremely high (belonging, identity, social acceptance are core human needs). Novelty is high (foreign environment, new language, unfamiliar social codes). Urgency is high (daily mocking, immediate peer pressure). Conduciveness is highly negative (-0.9) because the environment actively prevents acceptance and reinforces exclusion. Controllability is low (0.2) because Napoleon cannot change his accent, stature, or poverty overnight. Adjustability is minimal (0.1) because refusal to assimilate is a choice, not adaptive. Internal standards are strong (0.7) regarding excellence and Corsican identity. External standards are weak (0.3) because Napoleon rejects peer norms.

secondary.qualifier: approach through competitive excellence, not social connection
emotional avoidance; withdrawal from peer intimacy

sub_thoughts.text: I feel scorned, mocked, diminished by these boys
They mock me because I am Corsican, poor, small, and speak differently; these are unchangeable facts about my origin
Their rejection proves they are small-minded and beneath contempt; I will not degrade myself by conforming
I will surpass them through excellence in studies and become someone of such consequence that their mockery becomes irrelevant
I am fundamentally different from them and belong to a higher order; my foreignness is not a weakness but a mark of distinction
This isolation connects to my family's status, my father's death, my need to become head of household
If I soften, if I adapt, I lose myself and validate their judgment of my inferiority

memories.text: Napoleon studied obsessively not for love of learning but as a strategic weapon to surpass his tormentors, reading Caesar's commentaries, Plutarch's Lives, and histories of great military leaders to understand how to acquire and hold power.

Controllability is high (study is fully within his control). Adjustability is moderate (can vary study intensity but core goal is rigid). Internal standards are high (personal ambition to surpass rivals). External standards are low (formal education/tormentors do not validate this pathway).

Master the principles of power acquisition and military strategy so as to eventually surpass, dominate, or overcome those who currently torment
I am currently powerless but capable; my intelligence and discipline are superior tools; I can transform my status through systematic effort

memories.text: Napoleon graduated from École Militaire in 1785 ranked 42nd out of 58 students, a mediocre result he attributed to examiner prejudice against Corsicans rather than his own ability.

Adjustability low: cannot redo exam. Internal standards very high: Napoleon believes in his own merit. External standards low: he rejects examiner judgment as biased, so their standard carries little weight.

Prove the examiners wrong by rising through the artillery branch where mathematics and talent matter more than birth or ethnicity
I am capable of greatness despite institutional rejection; my destiny is not defined by this ranking

Dominance: moderate-low submission, as he is newly commissioned junior officer in hierarchical military structure despite internal conviction of destined superiority.

relationship.relationship_detail: Military institution is simultaneously enabler (meritocratic artillery path) and antagonist (examiner prejudice attributed to Corsican bias, hierarchy that limits junior lieutenant authority). Trust is conditional: institution accepted as vehicle for advancement, but not trusted to grant fair treatment without external pressure.

gut_feeling.resonance: burning ambition without object creates somatic restlessness; commission activates forward momentum but also visceral awareness of gap between current station and internal conviction of destiny

memories.pad_justification: Pleasure: moderate positive (achievement of commission, vindication through meritocratic path) tempered by awareness of mediocre graduation and physical inadequacy. Arousal: moderate-high activation reflecting the intensity of ambition, youthful energy, and the cognitive dissonance between aspiration and current station. Dominance: moderate-low submission, as he is newly commissioned junior officer in hierarchical military structure despite internal conviction of destined superiority.
memories.drive_justification: Curiosity: mildly activated (voracious reading mentioned in next phase, not yet foregrounded at commissioning). Competence: moderately strong delta—commission validates mathematical/technical mastery and meritocratic advancement, though junior rank limits scope. Affiliation: negative delta—physical shortness, Corsican status, and resentment of prejudice create distance from peer group and establishment. Autonomy: strong positive delta—artillery branch chosen for independence from birth-based hierarchy, and commission grants agency within military structure despite hierarchical constraint.
memories.confidence_justification: High confidence because biographical text explicitly states commission details, age, and Napoleon's own attributed interpretation of graduation result. Lower confidence (not 0.95) because internal emotional states ('burning with ambition') are inferred from contextual language rather than direct first-person testimony.

memories.text: During eight years of restless frustration (1785-1793), Napoleon served in garrisons, took leaves to Corsica, involved himself in Corsican politics, and wrote mediocre novellas and essays while voraciously reading Enlightenment philosophers.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is slightly negative due to the characterization as 'restless frustration' and 'mediocre' output, reflecting dissatisfaction with his station. Arousal is moderate (0.5) because he is actively engaged in reading, writing, and political involvement—not passive, but not in crisis. Dominance is low (-0.4) because he has limited control over his advancement; he is frustrated by constraints despite his ambition.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is high (0.9) because this period directly shapes his worldview and ambition. Novelty is moderate-low (0.4) because garrison life is routine, though reading philosophers offers some novelty. Urgency is moderate (0.6) because his sense of destiny creates pressure to find his form. Conduciveness is negative (-0.5) because the eight years feel like wasted time relative to his ambitions. Controllability is low (0.3) because he cannot control the path to greatness; adjustability is slightly higher (0.4) as he adapts by reading and writing. Internal standards are very high (0.8)—he knows he deserves greatness; external standards are low (0.2) because the aristocratic system doesn't recognize merit.

sub_thoughts.text: I feel restless and frustrated—I am burning with ambition but trapped in mediocrity and routine.
The existing order blocks my rise; talent is not recognized without birth, so the system itself is unjust.
My writing is mediocre, my posting is in the least fashionable branch, and my time in garrison is wasted potential.
I will immerse myself in reading to understand the world and find the path to my greatness.
I know I am destined for greatness, but the form is not yet clear—I am waiting for the moment to seize.
This period echoes my humiliation at Brienne, where I was mocked as a Corsican outsider.
What if this frustration lasts forever? What if I never find my true vocation?

cognitive.cognitive_distortions_justification: All-or-nothing thinking (0.7): he sees his output as 'mediocre' with no middle ground; his rank is 42/58 (middle of class) but he attributes it to prejudice rather than acknowledging his performance. Mind-reading (0.6): he assumes the examiners were biased against Corsicans without full evidence. Fortune-telling (0.65): he assumes he is 'destined for greatness' without rational basis—a speculative inference about the future.

drive_impact.drive_justification: Curiosity is boosted (0.8) by voracious reading of Enlightenment philosophers and intellectual engagement. Competence is reduced (-0.6) because his actual output (novellas, essays) is mediocre and his military rank is in the least fashionable branch, creating a gap between self-image and achievement. Affiliation is slightly reduced (-0.4) because garrison postings isolate him and his Corsican involvement separates him from French networks. Autonomy is significantly reduced (-0.7) because the aristocratic system constrains his rise; he has no control over the path to his 'destined' greatness.

confidence.confidence_justification: High confidence (0.75) because the passage provides explicit statements ('burning with ambition,' 'he knew he was destined for greatness,' 'restless frustration') and behavioral evidence (voracious reading, political involvement). Lower than 1.0 because the exact intensity of his frustration and the precise attribution to prejudice vs. actual mediocrity are reconstructed from the text rather than directly stated.

memories.text: Through reading Rousseau, Voltaire, Montesquieu, and Raynal, Napoleon developed a political philosophy combining Enlightenment rationalism with authoritarian instincts, coming to believe in meritocracy but rejecting democracy.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure: 0.7 — intellectual engagement with great works and coherent worldview formation is intrinsically satisfying. Arousal: 0.5 — reading and philosophical reflection are moderately engaging activities, neither passive nor acutely urgent. Dominance: 0.8 — the memory captures Napoleon synthesizing ideas into a personal philosophy that privileges control and hierarchy, reflecting high sense of mastery over intellectual material.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance: 0.95 — intellectual development directly supports Napoleon's burning ambition for greatness. Novelty: 0.7 — Enlightenment texts are intellectually novel, though synthesizing them into coherent philosophy reduces pure novelty. Urgency: 0.4 — reading is deliberate, not time-pressured. Conduciveness: 0.9 — the philosophy developed enables his later authoritarian actions and self-justification. Controllability: 0.85 — Napoleon actively selects and synthesizes ideas. Adjustability: 0.7 — once formed, this philosophy becomes relatively rigid (meritocracy yes, democracy no). Internal_standards: 0.95 — this aligns perfectly with his self-image as destined for greatness and capable of superior judgment. External_standards: 0.3 — his philosophy explicitly rejects democratic values and contradicts revolutionary egalitarianism, violating social norms of the period.

sub_thoughts.text: Intellectual stimulation and satisfaction from mastering great philosophical texts
Exposure to Rousseau, Voltaire, Montesquieu, and Raynal provided intellectual frameworks that aligned with pre-existing authoritarian instincts and meritocratic beliefs
The synthesized philosophy is logically coherent to Napoleon: meritocracy justifies his own rise despite low birth; authoritarianism justifies his conviction that strong will must govern
To use this intellectual framework to justify future consolidation of power and hierarchical governance
These readings confirm that Napoleon is not limited by social constraints — his superior intellect and will qualify him to rule, validating his sense of destiny

This intellectual work connects to his earlier humiliation at Brienne and École Militaire, where birth mattered more than merit — he is now constructing a philosophy where merit (his own) supersedes birth
Despite intellectual sophistication, the philosophy may be a rationalization for authoritarian impulses rather than genuine reasoned belief

cognitive.cognitive_distortions_justification: Mind reading (0.65): Napoleon assumes he knows what the Enlightenment philosophers intended and what their ideas 'really mean' for governance, filtering them through his own bias toward authoritarianism. Fortune telling (0.7): His belief that he is 'destined for greatness' and that his meritocratic philosophy will vindicate him is speculative projection onto the future. Emotional reasoning (0.6): His contempt for democracy and attraction to authoritarianism stem from emotional conviction (his humiliation at school, his sense of superiority) disguised as rational philosophy.

drive_impact.drive_justification: Curiosity +0.8: voracious reading of major philosophers directly activates and satisfies curiosity drive. Competence +0.85: mastering philosophical frameworks and synthesizing them into coherent worldview strongly activates competence drive. Affiliation -0.4: the meritocratic philosophy explicitly devalues collective democratic governance and emphasizes individual hierarchy, slightly suppressing affiliation drive in favor of separation. Autonomy +0.75: the philosophy justifies individual will and agency over collective constraint, supporting autonomy drive.

confidence.confidence_justification: The biographical text explicitly states what Napoleon read and what philosophy he developed, providing high evidential certainty. However, the internal experience of satisfaction, intensity, and whether reading was voracious from genuine curiosity or compensatory for his frustration must be inferred from context (his 'restless frustration,' his sense of destiny). The connection between reading and his later authoritarian actions is historically corroborated but not explicitly stated in this passage.

habituation.echoes: intellectual compensation for social humiliation at Brienne and École Militaire; formation of identity through reading (common in ambitious young men seeking self-definition); philosophical rationalization of pre-existing personality traits

cognitive.caps_inputs_justification: Achievement_opportunity (0.8): reading and philosophical synthesis represent clear intellectual achievement pathways. Skill_challenge (0.7): mastering complex philosophical texts and synthesizing them is cognitively challenging. Social_comparison (0.6): Napoleon's philosophy explicitly hierarchizes people by merit, suggesting ongoing comparison of self to others. Autonomy_choice_available (0.75): he autonomously selects which texts to read and how to interpret them. Autonomy_novelty_encountered (0.65): Enlightenment philosophy is genuinely novel intellectual territory. Threat_social_threat (0.35): his meritocratic philosophy is partially a defensive response to his rejection at École Militaire and Brienne, suggesting latent social threat.

memories.text: The French Revolution of 1789 thrilled Napoleon as destruction of the aristocratic order that had humiliated him at Brienne, promising that talent could rise without permission from birth.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is high (0.85) because the Revolution promised validation of his meritocratic beliefs and destruction of the system that humiliated him. Arousal is elevated (0.75) due to the passionate, intense nature of revolutionary promise and its personal significance. Dominance is moderately high (0.70) as he sees opportunity for his will to shape events, though not yet actualized.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is maximum (0.95) as this directly addresses his lifelong grievance and meritocratic ideology. Novelty is very high (0.90) — a revolution is unprecedented. Urgency is high (0.80) given the rapid, dramatic events. Conduciveness is positive (0.85) as it promises removal of barriers. Controllability is low (0.45) because events are unfolding beyond his current influence as a junior officer. Adjustability is low (0.40) as he cannot shape the Revolution's course yet. Internal standards align perfectly (0.95) with meritocracy promises. External standards are moderately aligned (0.70) with Enlightenment ideals, though social instability creates tension.

sub_thoughts.text: Thrilled excitement at the destruction of aristocratic humiliation system
The Revolution removes birthright barriers and validates his belief that talent should determine success
This is vindicating proof that the old order deserved destruction and that his resentment was justified
To position himself to rise through talent within this new meritocratic framework
I was right all along about my destiny; the world is finally arranged to recognize greatness
Echoes his reading of Rousseau and Enlightenment philosophers on natural inequality and merit
Underlying anxiety that despite promise, he still must prove himself and navigate uncertain revolutionary chaos

cognitive.cognitive_distortions_justification: Fortune-telling (0.75) evident in his certainty about destined greatness without yet knowing its form. All-or-nothing thinking (0.65) in viewing the Revolution as absolute vindication of his philosophy and complete destruction of an unjust order, without nuance about mixed motivations or outcomes.

drive_impact.drive_justification: Curiosity increases modestly (0.65) as revolution opens new possibilities. Competence increases substantially (0.80) as meritocratic pathway validates his self-assessment. Affiliation decreases significantly (-0.40) as he emphasizes his difference from and superiority to the masses. Autonomy increases greatly (0.75) as barriers to his rise are removed.

confidence.confidence_justification: The memory reports his felt emotion ('thrilled') directly (STATED as to feeling), but his underlying belief in destined greatness and interpretation of revolutionary events as personal vindication are inferred from his later actions and statements attributed to him. Confidence is moderate (0.70) because the source relies on biographical interpretation rather than direct testimony.

memories.text: Witnessing the storming of the Tuileries in August 1792—mobs killing Swiss Guards and dragging the royal family through jeering crowds—Napoleon felt contempt for the King's weakness rather than solidarity with the people, telling Bourrienne 'If I had been king, the rabble would never have entered.'
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is negative due to disgust at mob violence and royal weakness, not joy at revolutionary change. Arousal is high (0.8) because witnessing graphic violence (killing, dragging) and crowd chaos creates acute physiological activation. Dominance is elevated (0.7) because the memory crystallizes Napoleon's conviction that he would have controlled the situation through force—a sense of imagined mastery over chaos.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is extremely high (0.95): the event directly challenges Napoleon's emerging political philosophy and reveals the flaw he perceives in revolutionary governance. Novelty is high (0.8): mob violence on this scale is unprecedented in his experience. Urgency is acute (0.9): the threat to social order demands immediate cognitive integration. Conduciveness is positive (0.85) because the chaos confirms his belief system and validates his authoritarian convictions, enabling his worldview. Controllability is low (0.3): he cannot control mob behavior or royal response. Adjustability is minimal (0.2): the event is complete and unchangeable. Internal standards alignment is high (0.95): the event aligns perfectly with his belief in the necessity of strong authority. External standards alignment is near-zero (0.1): revolutionary ideology celebrates popular sovereignty, which contradicts his reaction.

sub_thoughts.text: Horror and revulsion at the spectacle of mob violence, not revolutionary exhilaration
The King failed to exercise overwhelming force; weakness of authority allows mob rule
The mob is rabble incapable of self-governance; the King was weak and deserved his fate
If I possessed power, I would crush such disorder with absolute authority
I am fundamentally different from both the mob and the failed King—I am the strong hand the world needs
This echoes the aristocratic contempt he experienced at Brienne, but inverted: now he sees the people as beneath order-making, not himself
If chaos like this spreads unchecked, society will collapse unless a man of will rises to restore order

cognitive.cognitive_distortions_justification: All-or-nothing (0.85): he frames the choice as absolute—either mob rule or authoritarian control, with no middle ground. Mind-reading (0.75): he asserts knowledge of the mob's incapacity for self-governance without evidence beyond this single event. Fortune-telling (0.7): he predicts that 'the rabble would never have entered' if he were king, a counterfactual certainty. Magnification (0.8): he elevates this single act of violence into proof that democracy is impossible and only strong authority can save civilization.

drive_impact.drive_justification: Curiosity decreases (delta -0.7) because the event forecloses intellectual openness to democratic theory—it 'confirms' his conviction, reducing need to explore further. Competence surges (delta +0.8) as witnessing chaos strengthens his conviction that he possesses the superior judgment and will to order it. Affiliation plummets (delta -0.9) because contempt for both mob and King severs emotional bond with the people and their cause. Autonomy increases (delta +0.6) as the spectacle of failed governance reinforces his belief that only he—unbound by mob opinion or aristocratic constraint—can act decisively.

confidence.confidence_justification: The memoir records Napoleon's direct statement ('If I had been king...') and his disgust, allowing high confidence (0.75) in his emotional reaction and stated belief. However, confidence is not 1.0 because psychological motivations (whether contempt masks fear, or stems from genuine conviction) are partly speculated, and the historical record does not exhaustively detail his internal state during August 1792.

memories.text: Within weeks of taking command, Napoleon transformed the demoralised Italian army through tactical brilliance, relentless energy, and inspirational rhetoric, promising soldiers access to fertile lands and rich provinces through military conquest.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is high: Napoleon experiences triumph through rapid transformation and vindication of his superiority over doubting officers. Arousal is elevated: the memory involves intense military activity, rapid change, and relentless energy deployment. Dominance is very high: he completely subordinates the army's will to his own through rhetorical manipulation and demonstrated tactical superiority.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is very high: proving his superiority is central to Napoleon's self-concept. Novelty is high: the speed of transformation exceeds typical military reorganisation. Urgency is high: the army's despair creates immediate pressure. Conduciveness is very positive: outcomes directly enable his larger ambitions. Controllability and adjustability are very high: his tactical and rhetorical tools work precisely as intended. Internal standards are met excellently: he validates his own assessment of his talent. External standards alignment is poor: the officers' initial contempt and the Directory's skepticism are disregarded or overcome through force of personality rather than institutional legitimacy.

sub_thoughts.text: Exultation at rapidly transforming contemptuous officers into devoted soldiers through tactical and rhetorical mastery
Success stems from combination of genuine tactical superiority, demonstrated energy, and manipulative rhetoric that frames looting as liberation
This transformation proves that his self-assessment of talent was correct and that the world's initial doubt was merely delayed recognition
Use this proven ability to build an increasingly dependent military apparatus and consolidate personal authority over institutional structures
Recognition that he possesses a gift for inspirational rhetoric bordering on manipulation—a capability distinct from tactical skill but equally effective
Links to earlier memory of officers' contempt based on age, stature, and Corsican origin—the transformation is simultaneously military achievement and personal vindication
The reliance on rhetoric and personality rather than institutional legitimacy creates long-term vulnerability if he loses access to victory narratives

Autonomy delta is positive: he demonstrates complete freedom from the officers' prior doubts and from Directory constraints.

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is high due to decisive military victory and earned affection; arousal is very high due to combat intensity, personal physical danger ('under fire'), and rapid successive battles demanding acute activation; dominance is high reflecting Napoleon's personal leadership, strategic control, and soldiers' deference ('le petit caporal').

sec.sec_justification: Relevance extremely high—military victory is core to Napoleon's ambitions. Novelty moderate-high; rapid audacious tactics were innovative for 1796. Urgency high; wartime context with Austrian/Sardinian opposition. Conduciveness strongly positive; victories advance strategic goals. Controllability high; Napoleon's personal leadership and tactical decisions drove outcomes. Adjustability moderate; battle conditions demand flexibility but core strategy remained sound. Internal standards very high; personal valor matches his ideals of leadership. External standards very high; contemporaries recognized legendary status.

memories.text: Each successive military victory in Italy confirmed Napoleon's sense of personal superiority and vindicated his belief that the world's estimation of talent was finally aligning with his own.

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is very high due to vindication and triumph over doubters; arousal is elevated (high-intensity victory context) but not extreme as these are repeated confirmations rather than novel shocks; dominance is near-maximum as each victory demonstrates Napoleon's control over events and people.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is maximal—military success directly confirms his core belief about talent alignment. Novelty is moderate because while each battle is distinct tactically, the pattern of vindication repeats. Urgency is moderate (military context demands immediate action). Conduciveness is very positive (victories enable his ambitions). Controllability is high as he orchestrates these victories. Internal standards are vastly exceeded (aligns perfectly with his self-assessment). External standards are low (society's prior dismissal of him as 'too young, too short, too Corsican' means he dismisses external judgment as retrograde).

sub_thoughts.text: Each victory produces intense joy and pride; a sense of being vindicated
Military victories prove that talent can now be recognized objectively; doubters were wrong about him
The world's prior dismissal of him was an error; these victories correct that error and prove his self-assessment was accurate
Continue pursuing battles and strategic victories to further entrench this vindication and accumulate more proof
He is the exceptional one; his early rejection by others was their failure of judgment, not his deficiency
Each victory echoes and reinforces the original wound of being underestimated—now healed through conquest
The need to maintain this vindication becomes self-perpetuating; stopping or losing would invalidate the narrative he is constructing

cognitive.cognitive_distortions_justification: All-or-nothing: victories are framed as complete vindication of his superiority, not as contextual military successes. Emotional reasoning: the feeling of triumph is treated as proof of objective superiority. Personalization: external events (battles, general dismissals) are interpreted as reflections on his personal worth rather than as independent military/administrative events.

memories.text: Napoleon systematically ignored orders from the Directory in Paris, marginalised their commissioners, negotiated unauthorised treaties, and reorganised Italian states without permission, leveraging his military indispensability to consolidate independent power.
memories.subject: Napoleon

memories.text: Napoleon experienced visceral satisfaction in reversing the power dynamic with Paris — the Directory had given him command as a consolation prize, but now they depended on him for survival.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is high due to the explicit 'pleasure that was almost physical' from dominating those who previously dismissed him. Arousal is moderately high (0.75 rather than extreme) because this is a sustained power reversal rather than acute crisis—it's savored rather than panicked. Dominance is very high (0.90) as the core of the memory is Napoleon's sudden control over Paris despite their nominal authority.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is very high—reversing power hierarchies was central to Napoleon's self-concept. Novelty is high (0.80) because military commanders rarely achieved such leverage over civilian government. Urgency is moderate (0.70) as this is a sustained shift, not acute. Conduciveness is positive (0.85) because the outcome aligns perfectly with his needs for recognition and control. Controllability is high (0.90) as he engineered the reversal through military success and threat. Adjustability is high (0.85) as he continues exploiting the dynamic. Internal standards are very high (0.95)—this confirms his self-belief in superiority. External standards are low (0.40) because this behaviour violates republican norms of civilian oversight and subordination.

sub_thoughts.text: Visceral satisfaction and almost-physical pleasure at the power reversal
Paris gave him command as a consolation prize (dismissive gesture), but his military success made them dependent on him
The reversal confirms that those who underestimated him were wrong and that he is indispensable
Continue exploiting this leverage—ignore orders, reorganise without permission, marginalise supervisors
This proves my superiority was always evident; the world's delayed recognition has finally arrived and is now irreversible
Echoes earlier humiliations: being dismissed as 'too young, too short, too Corsican' by the officer corps
Implicit worry that this power could be fragile if military success falters or if Paris finds a replacement

cognitive.cognitive_distortions_justification: All-or-nothing thinking (0.75): Napoleon frames the reversal as total vindication—Paris either depends on him or he is disposable; no middle ground. Mind-reading (0.70): He infers the Directory's desperation ('could not replace him') without explicit communication; assumes their entire survival depends on him alone. Emotional reasoning (0.65): The pleasure he feels is treated as proof of rightness and superiority, rather than examining the actual political fragility beneath.

drive_impact.drive_justification: Curiosity delta is near-zero (0.10) as this event confirms rather than opens new questions. Competence is strongly affirmed (0.85) by the military success that created the leverage. Affiliation is strongly negative (-0.75) as the memory reinforces his contempt for Paris and his need to dominate rather than cooperate. Autonomy is powerfully enabled (0.90) by the reversal—he now acts without Directory constraint.

confidence.confidence_justification: High confidence (0.90) because the text explicitly states 'the pleasure that was almost physical' and describes his actions (ignoring orders, marginalising commissioners, threatening resignation) as deliberate and knowing. memories.text: When General Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte displayed independent ambition and won a minor engagement without orders, Napoleon froze him out and reassigned him rather than acknowledging his success.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is high because Napoleon experiences satisfaction from suppressing a rival's success and reasserting control. Arousal is moderate-to-high because the situation involves active competitive engagement and tactical maneuvering. Dominance is very high as Napoleon consciously exerts power over Bernadotte by freezing him out and reassigning him.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is very high: Bernadotte's independent success directly threatens Napoleon's supremacy. Novelty is low: this pattern of suppressing rivals repeats throughout his career. Urgency is moderate-high: the threat must be contained quickly. Conduciveness is very negative: Bernadotte's success is incompatible with Napoleon's need for exclusive recognition. Controllability and adjustability are high: Napoleon has full authority to reassign officers. Internal and external standards are very low: Napoleon's ego-driven suppression violates norms of military merit recognition.

Napoleon intends to suppress Bernadotte's visibility and remove him from the theater where he might accumulate more independent success
This reveals Napoleon's deep insecurity despite outward confidence—he cannot tolerate others' competence because it threatens his narrative of unique superiority
This echoes the earlier theme of the Directory's commissioners being marginalized and the pleasure Napoleon takes in others' dependence on him
The suppression of Bernadotte foreshadows a broader pattern that will undermine Napoleon's long-term command structure by preventing talented subordinates from developing and creating resentment

Catastrophizing: He escalates a minor engagement win into an existential threat to his supremacy. Personalization: He interprets Bernadotte's actions as directed at him personally rather than as autonomous professional conduct.

Personalization: he interprets the officers' initial skepticism as a personal rejection of his worth rather than a contextual response to his unfamiliar leadership style. memories.text: Napoleon's rapid ascent in Italy from despised outsider to indispensable military commander who could defy civil authority became a formative demonstration that tactical brilliance, relentless drive, and inspirational manipulation could overcome both institutional resistance and personal prejudice.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is high due to Napoleon's sense of vindication and triumph over those who dismissed him; arousal is elevated because the Italian campaign involved constant military action, high-stakes decision-making, and confrontation with authority; dominance is extremely high as Napoleon progressively subjugated both enemies and superiors, culminating in defying the Directory itself.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is extremely high—this experience directly contradicts Napoleon's self-concept as underestimated; novelty is high because rapid military success and authority defiance were unprecedented in his career; urgency was elevated (military campaigns demand immediate action); conduciveness strongly positive (outcomes aligned with his desires); controllability high (tactical and rhetorical skill gave him agency); adjustability moderate (once committed to defiance, flexibility limited); internal standards strongly affirmed (vindication of self-belief); external standards severely violated (he disregarded Directory orders and institutional norms).

sub_thoughts.text: Napoleon felt euphoria and vindication as despised officers transformed into devoted followers and military victories accumulated.
His tactical genius, relentless energy, and manipulative rhetoric overcame initial prejudice; each victory proved his superiority and justified his self-belief.

He judged his ascent as proof that talent and willpower could overcome institutional resistance and personal dismissal; he assessed subordinates' independent success as threatening rather than complementary.
Continue expanding military and political power, eliminate rivals who show independent ambition, defy civilian authority when it constrains his objectives, consolidate his indispensability.
Napoleon's self-concept crystallized: he was exceptional—destined to lead—and the world's initial underestimation proved how blind institutions and ordinary men were to true talent.
This experience connected to his earlier sense of being an outsider (Corsican, short, young) and transformed that into evidence of special destiny rather than genuine disability.

The memory embeds a template for future threat-perception: successful subordinates became rivals to suppress rather than allies to develop; authority that questions him becomes an obstacle to overcome.

Mind-reading: Napoleon inferred that the Directory 'depended on him for survival' and 'could not replace him'—projecting his own logic onto their constraints. Personalization: officers' initial dismissal reframed as evidence of the world's injustice rather than reasonable skepticism based on age and appearance.

memories.text: Napoleon defeated the Mamluks at the Battle of the Pyramids but lost his fleet to Nelson at Aboukir Bay, stranding his army in Egypt and experiencing military setbacks in Syria.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is negative due to the net strategic failure despite initial victory; arousal is high due to the intensity of military conflict, tactical crisis, and the physiological stress of combat and stranding; dominance is reduced because the loss of fleet and failure to take Acre represent loss of control over circumstances.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance: extremely high—this directly threatens Napoleon's Alexandrine identity project. Novelty: moderate-high—losing a fleet to an enemy commander is not routine. Urgency: very high—stranding an army is an immediate crisis. Conduciveness: highly negative—the outcomes block the core goal of Eastern conquest. Controllability: moderate—tactical adaptation was possible but Nelson's victory was largely circumstantial. Adjustability: moderate—he pivoted to cultural/scientific framing. Internal standards: high—Napoleon has internalized an expectation of invincibility. External standards: high—European observers expect victorious conquest.

sub_thoughts.text: Simultaneous pride at defeating Mamluks and distress at losing fleet; the victory is eclipsed by the catastrophic loss.
Nelson's naval superiority and the failure to maintain supply lines caused the stranding; the Syria campaign failed due to fortified resistance at Acre.
The campaign is a stalemate dressed as achievement—real scholarly accomplishments (Description de l'Égypte) are tools to disguise military failure.
Reframe the military stalemate through cultural and scientific narrative; maintain face through propaganda rather than acknowledge strategic failure.

Napoleon recognizes that he is capable of tactical adaptation and can survive setbacks, but this experience will crystallize a belief that vulnerability (like betrayal by Joséphine) must be countered with armour and retaliation rather than introspection.

This military humiliation pairs with Joséphine's infidelity discovered during the same period, compounding the sense of loss of control and triggering a defensive posture toward both military and domestic domains.
The stranded army raises existential anxiety about retreat and abandonment; the failure to conquer Egypt threatens the Alexandrine mythology that anchors his identity.

Autonomy significantly reduced because stranding removes freedom of action and maneuver.

memories.text: Napoleon reflected on his experience in Egypt, recognizing that his response to Joséphine's infidelity taught him not empathy but emotional armour—a principle that would define his approach to intimate relationships.
memories.subject: Napoleon

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is negative due to the painful recognition of betrayal and the hardening response it triggered. Arousal is moderate—this is reflective cognition about past injury, not acute crisis, but the content carries emotional weight. Dominance is elevated because the reflection centers on adopting emotional control as a coping mechanism to prevent future vulnerability.

sec.sec_justification: Relevance is very high: infidelity strikes at core identity and relational values. Novelty is moderate—betrayal is a known human experience but felt as novel in personal context. Urgency is moderate because this is retrospective reflection, not active crisis. Conduciveness is strongly negative: infidelity blocks relationship goals and threatens attachment security. Controllability is high because Napoleon identifies a cognitive response strategy (emotional armour) within his control. Adjustability is moderately high: he can implement emotional distance. Internal standards are low because his response (hardening rather than reconnecting) violates relational intimacy norms he may have once held. External standards are moderate: society might endorse emotional resilience but judge coldness in marriage.

To protect future intimate relationships by maintaining psychological distance and control

Connects the Egypt experience to a lifelong pattern of treating intimacy as strategically managed rather than genuinely felt

memories.text: Napoleon abandoned his army of 30,000 men in Egypt in August 1799, justifying the decision by claiming France needed him more than Egypt did, despite knowing the abandoned soldiers would eventually surrender to the British.
memories.subject: Napoleon Bonaparte

pad.pad_justification: Pleasure is moderately positive because Napoleon felt justified and decisive about his choice; arousal is high (0.75) due to the high-stakes strategic decision and secret departure involving risk of discovery; dominance is very high (0.85) as he asserted control over his own destiny and prioritized his needs over his army's welfare.

sec.sec_justification: The decision is highly relevant to Napoleon's career and extremely urgent (Directory collapsing). Conducive to his goal of seizing power (0.8). He feels controllable of his own choice (0.85) but adjustability is limited—once he abandons the army, retrieval is impossible. Internal standards support ambition (0.7) but external standards are violated (0.3)—abandoning 30,000 soldiers is ethically questionable.

sub_thoughts.text: Felt confident, ambitious, and justified in the decision
France's political weakness created an urgency that only he could resolve; Egypt represented a sunk cost compared to the opportunity at home
